title: Why do leaves change color?
subtitle: Autumn & pigments
subject: sciences
description: Autumn does not invent colors: it removes the green that masked them. Behind the show, a survival strategy to get through the winter.

hero.hook: Autumn leaves don't put on makeup: they take off the green.

blocks.text: Every fall, the forests change from green to gold, to copper, to purple. This is not an aesthetic whim. It's a strategy: the tree recovers what it can before dropping its leaves for the winter.
Warm colors don't appear out of nowhere. Often, they were already there, hidden under the green. Understanding autumn means understanding a major biochemical cleaning.

From spring to late summer, leaves are full of **chlorophyll**, the pigment that fuels photosynthesis. It degrades under the light, but the tree constantly replaces it. As long as it dominates, the leaf remains green.

blocks.caption: In autumn, the chlorophyll disappears and reveals the colors of the leaves.

blocks.text: However, the leaf also contains **carotenoids**, yellow and orange pigments (like in carrots). In summer, they are there, but invisible under the green. In the fall, chlorophyll production stops. The green fades, the yellow and orange are revealed.
“Chlorophyll” comes from the Greek *chloros* (green) and *phyllon* (leaf). “Carotenoid” shares the root of… the carrot, where this pigment was first identified.

sections.title: The real trigger: the nights that get longer

blocks.text: It's not mainly the cold that kicks off autumn, but the length of the nights. Trees measure it using light sensors, the . When the nights get longer, a hormonal signal goes to each leaf. [[phytochromes]]

At the base of the petiole a [[The separation zone (abscission)]] forms, a sort of cap. The sap rises less, the sugars come down poorly. Isolated, the leaf degrades its chlorophyll more quickly. The more stable yellows remain for a few weeks, then the leaf falls.

sections.title: Where do the bright reds come from?

blocks.text: The yellow was already there. Red and purple are often **made** at the end of the season. These are , produced when sugars remain trapped in the leaf. [[Anthocyanins]]

Why invest energy just before throwing away the paper? Probably to protect **** during recycling. The tree recovers **azine** and other valuable nutrients. Without chlorophyll, the sun can damage still active tissues. Anthocyanins act as a solar filter during the big move towards the roots.

The most beautiful reds are often born from sunny days and cool, frost-free nights. Lots of sugar, transformation into anthocyanins. A gray and rainy autumn gives duller shades. An early frost kills the leaves before the show.

In the end, all that remains is the [[tannins]], brown substances from the forest floor. Some studies also think that bright colors warn the [[aphids]]: fit tree, strong defenses, better to go elsewhere.
Autumn reveals the yellows already present when chlorophyll disappears, and sometimes makes red to protect nutrient recycling before leaf fall.
